name: Distributed System
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Many Machines Pretending to Be One
lesson.summary: A distributed system is a collection of independent computers coordinating over an unreliable network to behave like a single coherent system, and the difficulty of that coordination is the root of why blockchains need consensus mechanisms at all.
lesson.body:
At its most basic, a distributed system is simply a collection of independent computers, connected by a network, that work together to appear as one coherent system to whoever is using it. This is a broader category than peer-to-peer networks specifically. A peer-to-peer network is one particular architecture for a distributed system, where participants communicate directly with each other as equals, but distributed systems also include architectures with some central coordination, like a cluster of servers behind a load balancer that still counts as distributed because the work is spread across multiple independent machines even though clients experience it as one service.

What makes distributed systems genuinely hard, in a way that is easy to underestimate, comes down to basic network fundamentals. Messages between independent machines take time to travel, and that travel time is not fixed or predictable, it varies with congestion, distance, and hardware. Messages can also be lost entirely, arrive out of order, or in rare cases be duplicated. Any two machines in a distributed system, even ones sitting in the same data center, cannot assume they see the same information at the same instant, because there is always some delay, however small, in getting information from one to the other. This basic physical reality is the root cause of most of the hard problems in distributed computing.

A further complication, especially relevant to systems that need to be trustworthy rather than merely functional, is that individual machines in a distributed system can fail in more troubling ways than simply going offline. A machine might crash and stop responding, which is relatively easy to detect and route around. But a machine might also behave arbitrarily: sending different, even contradictory information to different peers, whether due to a bug, hardware fault, or deliberate malice. This is called a Byzantine fault, and systems designed to tolerate it, called Byzantine fault tolerant systems, have to be built assuming some participants might actively lie rather than just fail silently.

This is where the earlier chapters in this book converge. A blockchain is, structurally, a distributed system: many independent nodes, connected over a peer-to-peer network, each holding a copy of the same hash chained, Merkle tree organized ledger, trying to agree on one consistent version of history despite unreliable message delivery and the possibility that some participants are actively dishonest. Decentralized trust is the goal, but achieving it requires solving the distributed systems problem of getting many independent, occasionally lying or unreliable machines to agree on a single shared truth, without any centralized trust anchor to simply declare the answer. Every consensus mechanism examined later in this book, whatever its specific design, is ultimately an engineered answer to that one underlying question: how do independent machines, talking over an unreliable network, come to agree on what actually happened.
